comments.comment: I'd expect #[inline] on Ord and Eq, maybe Clone, but having it on Debug is surprising. I put #[cold] on my fn fmt implementations!
comments.comment_plain: I'd expect `#[inline]` on `Ord` and `Eq`, maybe `Clone`, but having it on `Debug` is surprising. I put `#[cold]` on my `fn fmt` implementations!

comments.comment: For what it's worth this 2023 PR is the one that added #[inline] to Debug because it generally resulted in better (!) benchmark numbers. Interestingly, there was an experimental PR that only emitted the attribute on structs with <=5 fields and it resulted in a performance regression compared to always emitting the attribute.
comments.comment_plain: For what it's worth [this 2023 PR](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/117727) is the one that added `#[inline]` to `Debug` because it generally resulted in *better* (!) benchmark numbers. Interestingly, [there was an experimental PR that only emitted the attribute on structs with <=5 fields](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/118031) and it resulted in a performance regression compared to always emitting the attribute.

comments.comment: I suspect part of the reason is that many debug impls never get called, and by adding #[inline] we avoid ever codegen'ing them.
comments.comment_plain: I suspect part of the reason is that many debug impls never get called, and by adding `#[inline]` we avoid ever codegen'ing them.

comments.comment: Feels like a limitation resulted from Rust's proc macros operating on tokens instead of actual types. If the macros have type information they can look like how many levels of nested inlines there are and stop adding #[inline] if it's too deep.
comments.comment_plain: Feels like a limitation resulted from Rust's proc macros operating on tokens instead of actual types. If the macros have type information they can look like how many levels of nested inlines there are and stop adding `#[inline]` if it's too deep.

comments.comment: This seems worth a bugreport in the rust-lang/rust repo. We've changed the #[inline] on Debug in the past and we can change it again. It's just hard to pick a good trade-off between code size, compile time, and run time.

comments.comment:
#[inline] is just a hint

This is not quite true. It also enables cross-crate inlining, which is always possible for generics but not possible for non-generic functions by default. It's too bad we don't have a #[can_inline] that omits the hint part.
comments.comment_plain:
> `#[inline]` is just a hint

This is not quite true. It also *enables* [cross-crate inlining](https://matklad.github.io/2021/07/09/inline-in-rust.html#Inlining-in-Rust), which is always possible for generics but not possible for non-generic functions by default. It's too bad we don't have a `#[can_inline]` that omits the hint part.

I'd actually go on stop further and would like to see the compiler speculatively mark things as #[can_inline].

comments.comment:
The notion that it’s bad to say #[inline(always)] and you should say at most #[inline] is my least favorite Rust code review meme. Debugging time is expensive: It’s bad to have to see performance fail and only then after proving that you need #[inline(always)] to be allowed to say so instead of just #[inline].

If you know something is designed on the assumption that it need to be inlined to achieve perf targets, just put #[inline(always)] on it without proving that #[inline] wouldn’t suffice.
